clusters.text: The story that James Talarico was treated at Lindner Center of Hope or a mental health facility is false.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The Lindner Center of Hope publicly stated on Oct. 11 that 
"Representative James Talarico has never received treatment from Lindner Center of Hope."
 Talarico posted that 
"I've never even been to Ohio"
. He also told the Dallas Morning News editorial board he was 
not absent for mental health care and was home in bed with the flu
. The rumor rested on an unverified audio recording of a call that influencers Nick Sortor and Rhein Amacher posted. Snopes found the claimed discharge timing 
didn't match Talarico's schedule
. It also reviewed visual evidence, which it did not publish, 
that Talarico was at his Austin home every day of his flu
. Snopes, PolitiFact and FactCheck.org each rated or answered the claim as false or "No." One caveat is that the facility told the Daily Wire it 
does not confirm or deny whether any individual is or has been a patient
. That is a general policy line and sits alongside its specific public denial. The wider "or a mental health facility" wording can't be disproved in absolute terms. Still, no credible evidence supports it, and the fact-checkers' findings and the timeline point against it.

clusters.text: James Talarico was in a mental health facility, the Lindner Center, during his absence.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The claim is contradicted by the evidence. 
The Lindner Center posted on social media that Talarico "has never received treatment from Lindner Center of Hope."
 Talarico 
reshared that post and wrote that he has "never even been to Ohio."
 The claim traces back to an influencer's audio recording of a phone call. 
The Texas Tribune reports that Rhein Amacher said he called the center posing as Talarico's cousin and made up a patient code.
 PolitiFact found that the call's timeline 
conflicts with Talarico's public appearances on Oct. 9 and Oct. 10
, and rated it Pants on Fire. The AP also reported that 
images it reviewed showed Talarico at home over several days
. Snopes, FactCheck.org and the Dallas Morning News also rated the claim false. Talarico says he was at home with the flu. Reporting notes that the Lindner Center says it does not confirm or deny patients, but it did issue an explicit denial about Talarico.

clusters.text: A Lindner Center of Hope employee or psychiatric hospital said James Talarico was recently discharged.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The claim comes from an Oct. 11 X post by Nick Sortor and Rhein Amacher. It included an audio recording of a woman who said she was at the Lindner Center of Hope and that Talarico was just discharged. 
Amacher wrote that the caller identified herself as a female facility employee and said Talarico had been discharged within the previous 24–48 hours.
 Nobody has verified the caller's identity or role. 
The Lindner Center itself said that evening that Talarico "has never received treatment" there.
 
Talarico told the Dallas Morning News editorial board he was at home with the flu.
 The hospital did not say he was discharged. It said the opposite. Fact-checkers found no credible evidence for the claim. 
Snopes said it reviewed visual evidence, which it did not publish for privacy reasons, that Talarico was at his Austin home every day of his illness.
 Snopes rated the claim False. 
PolitiFact rated the related claim that the audio proves a discharge on Oct. 10 "Pants on Fire."
 
FactCheck.org also answered "No" and said the center rebutted the rumors.
 The only support is an unauthenticated recording, which the facility and the candidate both contradict.

James Talarico said only the child can determine a child's gender identity.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The Daily Wire reviewed a Texas House Juvenile Justice and Family Issues Committee hearing. 
It reports Talarico said, "There's only one person who can determine a child's gender identity, and that's the child."
 Breitbart repeats the same quote (
"only one person who can determine a child's gender identity, and that's the child"
). Both are partisan outlets, and I found no primary transcript or neutral news report that reproduces the line. Neutral coverage of the same 2019 hearing on HB 1910 (Fox via Yahoo, Hannity's transcript, and PolitiFact's summary of the ad) quotes only his "abusive" remarks about denying a child's gender identity. The Daily Wire's account has Talarico clarifying that 
"I don't think gender identity is something people can see differently,"
 which means the sentence was part of a longer exchange whose context I couldn't see. The paraphrase "only the child can determine a child's gender identity" matches the reported wording and is probably accurate. It rests on one outlet's account of the video, and I couldn't confirm it against the hearing record. The claim also leaves out the date (2019) and the setting (a debate over custody and child-abuse law).

clusters.text: James Talarico's campaign has stopped actively planning events in the final stretch of the race.
clusters.verdict_basis: Talarico did stop appearing in person for about 12 days. CNN and NBC News reported that his last in-person Texas event was Sept. 26. The Dallas Morning News reported that at least two events were scrapped: an Oct. 5 event for Black voters and an Oct. 6 Austin fundraiser. The campaign said the cause was the flu. It said he had held 100+ public events and would return soon. His calendar showed no candidate appearances, only canvassing, phone banks and get-out-the-vote gatherings (Townhall, Hot Air). The claim goes further than this. It says the campaign "stopped actively planning events in the final stretch." But the campaign kept scheduling field events. It also kept a CNN/Jubilee town hall set for Oct. 14. By Oct. 14, CNN reported he had returned to public events over the weekend, including Austin City Limits. The records back a temporary illness-related pause in his in-person appearances and some cancellations. They don't back a campaign-wide halt to event planning, so the claim as worded is misleading.

clusters.verdict_basis:

fieldwork on October 9–11, 2026, with 854 likely voters and a ±3.6 margin of error
